newsitem.title: USA: POLL - US yield curve gets the squeeze through '98.
newsitem.headline: POLL - US yield curve gets the squeeze through '98.

text.p: U.S. long-term interest rates probably will peak sometime in the third quarter as U.S. credit markets anticipate a pickup in economic growth, according to economists polled by Reuters.

Short-term yields should follow suit as many of the survey respondents projected an increase in the federal funds target rate before year-end. Twenty-eight experts surveyed on Tuesday and Wednesday forecast the average two-year note yield would rise to 6.36 percent by January 1998 and slide to 6.34 percent by July next year.
Similarly, the experts projected the bellwether 30-year T-bond yield would show a more modest increase to 6.88 percent by January before slipping to 6.78 percent a year from now.
That would assume a spread of about 52 basis points between the two issues by year-end, dipping to about a 44-basis-point gap by the summer of 1998.
The current spread between the two- and 30-year issues is about 70 basis points.
"The (Treasury) market is becoming less volatile, so the (flattening) makes sense," said Matthew Alexy, chief Treasury market strategist at Credit Suisse First Boston Corp.
There are two different ways to smooth the curve, he explained.

A restrictive stance on monetary policy is one way, because the short end of the curve would rise faster than the long end, said Alexy. Another way is a neutral Fed coupled with a stable inflationary environment, he added.
Currently, it appears the economy is expanding at a slower clip from the 5.9-percent annualized growth rate in the first quarter, and inflationary pressures have yet to surface, analysts said.
The current economic scenario has most Wall Street economists expecting no move in interest rates when the Fed concludes its two-day monetary policy meeting on Wednesday.
Some experts said a pickup in growth in the second half of the year would prompt the central bank to boost rates at least one more time before year-end.
"In the third quarter you get ... robust economic activity which would justify another tightening before year-end," said Anthony Chan, chief economist of Banc One Investment Advisors Corp in Ohio.
An eventual rise in short-term rates should slow the economy on a longer-term basis, which would justify the flattening of the yield curve, he added.
Full results of the survey follow.
